# JusPrin production documentation

This directory is the canonical starting point for production work on `jusprin-newui`. It preserves the durable product and engineering decisions from `jusprin-v2-poc` without importing the POC's temporary windows, probes, static mocks, generated evidence, or environment-gated startup paths.

Read these documents in order:

1. [Product definition](product-definition.md) — the human/agent boundary, required product surfaces, workflow, and visibility rules.
2. [Production architecture](architecture.md) — the selected native/WebView architecture, ownership rules, component boundaries, and implementation sequence.
3. [Engineering and verification method](engineering-method.md) — how to assess risk and what evidence is required before calling a feature complete.
4. [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) — known Orca behaviors, lifecycle traps, event and history constraints, and testing lessons.
5. [Fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md) — required before changing any OrcaSlicer-owned file: where a seam belongs, why additive beats rewritten, how to leave a conflict that resolves correctly, and what evidence a change must record.
6. [Design system](design-system.md) — brand behavior, semantic UI tokens, typography, spacing, accessibility, and asset rules.
7. [POC reference](poc-reference.md) — exact pointers to the spike-only documents, code, commits, logs, screenshots, and generated brand artifacts left on `jusprin-v2-poc`.
8. [Tool extension guide](mcp-tool-extension-guide.md) — shared Agent/MCP contracts, process-settings workflow, execution and verification requirements.
9. [Local autosave and version history](autosave-version-history.md) — managed project storage, migration, restore, export, retention, and failure behavior.

Printer UI without hardware (Bambu in-process fake; control file; isolated app): [Fake Bambu README](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md). Print-host (Klipper/Moonraker) simulation stays on `jusprin-newui-fakeprinter`.

## Governing decisions

- JusPrin is an AI-piloted 3D-printing product built on OrcaSlicer, not a replacement slicing engine.
- OrcaSlicer's C++ model, slicing pipeline, viewport, geometry operations, project serialization, and undo stack remain authoritative.
- The production application stays native C++/wxWidgets/OpenGL. The Agent conversation uses a local React/TypeScript application inside `wxWebView`.
- JavaScript renders state and submits typed commands; it never owns editable Orca project state.
- When logic could live in either C++ or a React page, it goes in the page unless there is a strong reason for C++: it touches Orca state, enforces a limit or boundary the app must guarantee, has to work without a page, or needs a thread or lifetime the page lacks. See [Where logic goes](architecture.md#where-logic-goes-the-page-first).
- Product policy lives in fork-owned files. OrcaSlicer-owned files receive only small, product-neutral, additive seams — every line changed there is a line this fork re-resolves at every rebase.
- The user owns physical facts, object meaning, desired outcomes, privacy and legal decisions, and starting consequential physical actions.
- The production branch must not import experimental POC behavior merely because it demonstrated feasibility. Use the POC as evidence and reimplement through stable production boundaries.

## Source lineage

`jusprin-newui` and `jusprin-v2-poc` share base commit `8500fcdcca` (`v2.4.2`). The POC reference is pinned to final POC commit `9bba835b92`, so future changes to branch names do not make the historical evidence ambiguous.

# JusPrin production architecture

**Status:** This is the architecture chosen for the `jusprin-newui` branch. It also says where production code may and may not reach into OrcaSlicer.

JusPrin replaces what OrcaSlicer looks like and how people move through it. It keeps everything OrcaSlicer already does well to turn a model into a print. Product work should make it easier for people to say what they want and to check a print before sending it. It must not create JusPrin's own version of slicing, geometry, rendering, picking (working out which object the pointer is on), saving and loading, or undo history.

## Product composition

The project window we are building toward has four regions that stay in place:

1. A compact row that shows the printer and the project status.
2. A thin pane that lists plates and objects and can be collapsed.
3. OrcaSlicer's existing Prepare canvas (the 3D view).
4. A fixed pane that holds the Agent conversation and the print plan.

The compact plates/objects pane is deferred to a later task. The first
production shell and the first Agent implementation must not depend on it.
Until the pane is added, people work with objects through the native canvas
and the Agent.

Prepare is the screen people stay on. **Check print** opens a modal window. That window holds a second copy of OrcaSlicer's real Preview widget and shows the current valid slice of the active plate. OrcaSlicer's original Preview stays where it was, in `Plater`'s Notebook (OrcaSlicer's tabbed container). A small factory function on `Plater`, with nothing JusPrin-specific in it, gives that window the existing model, bed, slicing process, and G-code result. Closing the window returns focus to Prepare. The window also closes by itself when the project or the slice changes. **Print** currently opens OrcaSlicer's existing send confirmation dialog. It never sends straight away. Project details open as a drawer. Monitor is a separate screen that can stay visible while the person does other work.

## Runtime architecture

```text
OrcaSlicer process (C++17 / wxWidgets / OpenGL)
├── JusPrin application shell
│   ├── compact top navigation and machine status
│   ├── native plates/objects pane
│   ├── center workspace host
│   │   └── existing GLCanvas3D Prepare canvas
│   └── wxWebView
│       └── local React/TypeScript Agent interface
├── modal Check print window with Orca G-code Preview
├── typed workspace/controller boundary
├── existing Orca model, selection, plates, gizmos, and undo stack
└── existing slicing, project I/O, device, and print subsystems
```

The split between native code and web code is deliberately cautious:

- The 3D view, and anything drawn on top of it, stays native.
- The top row and the object/plate pane start as native wxWidgets.
- C++ owns the application state and the project state.
- The WebView receives versioned events and sends versioned commands.
- We may later try building the object pane in a WebView, but only as a change to how that one pane is drawn. It would not be a reason to move to Electron or to a WebGL 3D view.

## Authoritative ownership

For each kind of state, one part of the system holds the real copy. This table says which part, and what JusPrin does with that state.

| Concern | Authoritative owner | JusPrin responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Project model and object identity | Orca `Model` and `ObjectID` | Show a typed view that is valid only for the current project session |
| Plates and active plate | Orca `PartPlateList` | Show them, and ask for changes through commands |
| Selection and picking | Orca `Selection` and `GLCanvas3D` | Keep the UI in sync without creating feedback loops |
| Geometry transforms | Orca gizmos and `GizmoObjectManipulation` | Start the existing behavior and show exact values |
| Undo and redo | Orca undo stack | Report whether undo and redo are available and what they did. Keep no second undo stack |
| Slicing and Preview | Orca slicing actions and Preview canvas | Show the states of Slice and Check print |
| Project serialization | Orca 3MF and model serializers | Keep files compatible. Add migration only for new data |
| Agent conversation | React/TypeScript WebView | Render messages, write the words people and the model read, and submit typed commands (see [Where logic goes](#where-logic-goes-the-page-first)) |
| Agent print plan | C++/agent application boundary | Explain intent, decisions, uncertainty, and consequences |

## Production integration boundaries

### Shell host

The shell is the JusPrin window frame around OrcaSlicer's content. Build one shell, in files this fork owns, and attach it to `MainFrame` in one small place. Decisions about what happens at startup go in a bootstrap or a shell factory that the fork owns. Do not spread environment checks through OrcaSlicer's constructors.

The first production version may still construct OrcaSlicer's old top bar, tab panel, Sidebar, and `GUI_ObjectList` where existing OrcaSlicer beh

... [16814 characters truncated] ...

; the provider's prompt cache depends on the text staying byte-identical. The app has no default text. A turn the app starts itself before the page has sent the prompt (the first message after a file opens, or Ask AI on a print issue, while the page is still loading) waits in the reply queue and starts when the prompt arrives. The prompt lived in C++ until 2026-10-14 so that the MCP server's instructions could share part of it; they stopped sharing it on 2026-10-10. The MCP server's own instructions (`Mcp/McpProtocol.cpp`) and the request that names a conversation stay in C++: MCP has no page, and the title request is the app's own.

Windows uses WebView2, macOS uses WKWebView, and Linux uses WebKitGTK. The way the page's files are packaged must work on all three. The prototype packed the whole page into a single local file, because WKWebView failed to load additional files referenced through `file:` URLs. Production keeps the single-file approach, and CMake now builds that file from the TypeScript/React sources.

MCP (Model Context Protocol, which lets external AI tools call the app) and wider agent autonomy are layers that come after this one. They must go through the same typed workspace interface. They must not change who owns the 3D view.

### Gizmo presentation

Start with Move or Rotate. Build one reusable native controller that wraps the existing behavior:

1. Show a compact strip of tool buttons in the upper-left corner of the Prepare canvas. The strip is a horizontal row like OrcaSlicer's own toolbar, but aligned to the left instead of centred. The strip stays put when the selection or the camera moves, because a strip attached to the object would jump every time the view orbits. `Canvas/ViewportToolStrip` draws the strip with ImGui as part of the canvas's own frame, through `GLCanvas3D::set_overlay_renderer`. On every frame it asks the gizmo manager which tool is open. The open tool's values appear below the row in `Canvas/ToolValuePanel`, lined up with the button that opened the tool.
2. Activate the existing native gizmo.
3. Keep the existing pointer dragging, snapping, and selection behavior.
4. Send exact typed-in numbers through `GizmoObjectManipulation`.
5. Keep the existing timing of undo snapshots, and the existing undo and redo.
6. Closing a tool only closes it. Do not invent a draft that can be thrown away. Undo stays the way to revert a change, unless the product requirements explicitly change that.

After that, convert the remaining tools in groups that work in a similar way: Move/Rotate/Scale; Mirror/Duplicate/Place on face; Measure; Cut/Repair; Text/Emboss; painter-based tools.

### Semantic annotations

Semantic annotations are labels a person puts on part of a model to say what that part means, such as a face that must stay smooth. Reuse what OrcaSlicer's painting tools already do: raycasting, brush selection, clipping, showing painted facets, copying, undo, and saving into the 3MF file. Two things are not yet proven for production: labels with arbitrary meanings, and how those labels are presented to the agent. The first implementation should use two labels on one object. Before adding more labels, check that those two survive save and reload, transforms, duplication, undo and redo, and changes to the mesh's topology.

## Non-negotiable constraints

- Do not change slicing algorithms to make the UI easier to build.
- Do not replace `GLCanvas3D` or the G-code Preview.
- Do not reimplement geometry operations in TypeScript.
- Do not place WebView content over the native GL canvas.
- Do not keep a second copy of the project model or of the undo stack in JavaScript.
- Preserve 3MF projects, printer profiles, shortcuts, serialization, and cross-platform behavior.
- Do not try to match every stock OrcaSlicer feature when the product definition does not require it.
- Do not reopen the Electron or WebGL question without a new, explicit product decision backed by evidence.

## Implementation order

1. Write the canonical product documents, and set up the design tokens and the curated assets.
2. Bring the workspace interface up to production quality: the interface itself, commands that go through OrcaSlicer's own code, change observation, and tests against the real adapter.
3. Bring the canvas presentation API and its controller up to production quality.
4. Build the production shell without a compact object/plate pane.
5. Build the typed Agent WebView and the bridge between the page and the app.
6. Add the presentation controller for Move/Rotate, then convert the other groups of gizmos.
7. Add semantic annotations, Check print reporting, Send preflight, Monitor, calibration, and troubleshooting screens as the product definition describes them.
8. Add the compact object/plate pane as a separately planned task when it is prioritized.

Older implementations and the detailed evidence are deliberately left out of this document. See [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

# JusPrin product definition

**Status:** Canonical product direction for the `jusprin-newui` production branch.

**Source:** Consolidated from product discovery on `jusprin-v2-poc`. Historical inspection evidence remains on that branch; see [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

## Executive summary

An AI agent can remove much of a slicer’s technical complexity, but it cannot eliminate the need for user interaction.

The boundary is:

> The user tells the system what is physically true, what the object means, and what outcome is wanted. The agent chooses the technical printing strategy. The user verifies consequential decisions and remains in control of the physical machine.

This produces three classes of OrcaSlicer features:

1. **User-decision surfaces must remain prominent.**
   These capture information the agent cannot reliably obtain: physical setup, functional intent, geometry meaning, aesthetic preferences, legal restrictions, and control over real-world actions.

2. **Shared agent-and-user surfaces should be redesigned.**
   The agent proposes a solution, explains it, and draws attention to uncertainty. The user reviews the result visually instead of manipulating dozens of parameters.

3. **Implementation settings can disappear from the primary interface.**
   The agent can usually manage line widths, speeds, infill mechanics, cooling, retraction, support parameters, and similar technical details.

The final product should therefore retain nine primary surfaces:

1. Project knowledge
2. Physical setup
3. Print intent
4. Objects and plates
5. Essential geometry editing
6. Local meaning and overrides
7. Print-plan verification
8. Print preflight and live control
9. Calibration and troubleshooting

These are not remnants of a legacy slicer. They are the information and control boundary between a person, an AI agent, and a physical manufacturing process.

The interface should not give every retained feature equal weight. Features fall into four visibility levels:

1. **Default** — continuously visible in an ordinary project.
2. **Contextual** — appears when the project, current selection, or agent uncertainty makes it relevant.
3. **On demand** — available through Project details, More, or the expert layer.
4. **Interruptive** — normally hidden, but made prominent when a consequential warning, mismatch, or unresolved decision occurs.

Frequency alone does not determine visibility. A control can be rarely used but interruptive because overlooking it would be costly or unsafe.

---

# 1. Why an AI agent sometimes lacks enough information

Before deciding which UI to retain, it helps to distinguish the different reasons an agent cannot safely make a decision.

## 1.1 The agent cannot observe physical reality reliably

A slicer may say that a particular nozzle, plate, or filament is selected, but that does not prove it is installed.

Examples include:

- The build plate was changed manually.
- The AMS contains a different spool than expected.
- Filament is wet, old, tangled, or nearly empty.
- A hardened nozzle was replaced with a standard nozzle.
- Glue was or was not applied.
- The print bed is occupied.
- A previous print remains attached to the plate.

The agent can detect some of these conditions using printer sensors or a camera, but uncertainty must remain visible.

## 1.2 The agent does not know what the geometry means

A mesh contains shapes, not intentions.

The agent may identify a hole, thin wall, flat face, or overhang, but it does not inherently know whether that feature is:

- A precision bearing surface
- A screw hole
- A snap fit
- A decorative opening
- A sacrificial support
- A face that must remain smooth
- A surface hidden after assembly
- A region intended to flex
- A deliberately thin membrane

This is why essential geometry editing and semantic annotation must remain.

## 1.3 The agent does not know the user’s priorities

There is rarely one objectively correct slicing strategy. A user may prioritize:

- Appearance
- Strength
- Dimensional accuracy
- Speed
- Material savings
- Heat resistance
- Flexibility
- Watertightness
- Minimal support marks
- A particular color arrangement

These priorities can conflict. The agent needs the user to define what “good” means.

## 1.4 Some decisions are subjective

Seam placement, surface texture, layer visibility, support scars, color boundaries, and acceptable print time are personal judgments.

An agent can recommend an option, but it cannot determine the user’s taste from the model alone.

## 1.5 Some actions have consequential real-world effects

Starting a print consumes material, occupies a machine, creates heat and motion, and may run unattended for hours. Firmware updates and calibration changes can alter the behavior of the printer.

The agent can prepare these actions, but the user needs final authority over them.

## 1.6 Some information concerns ownership, law, or safety

The agent cannot invent or silently change:

- Authorship
- Licensing
- Commercial-use permission
- Safety warnings
- Assembly instructions
- Bill-of-materials information
- Intended use
- Privacy and cloud-connectivity preferences

These are authoritative project facts, not slicing parameters.

---

# 2. The surfaces that must remain

## 2.0 Project-window hierarchy

The Project window should not treat Prepare, Preview, and Info as three equal destinations.

---

## 2.9 Print preflight

This surface answers: **Is the correct job about to be sent to the correct physical machine?**

Prepare should contain a visible Print entry point. Print opens this preflight; it does not bypass it:

`Print -> Send preflight -> explicit Send`

The current Print action opens Orca's existing Select Machine or printer-host send dialog, which requires a separate send/upload choice. The complete JusPrin preflight checklist below remains future product work.

### What should remain

- Job name and thumbnail
- Destination printer
- Selected plate
- Time and material estimate
- Filament and AMS mapping
- Plate-type confirmation
- Bed-leveling choice
- Flow-calibration choice
- Timelapse choice
- First-layer inspection
- Build-plate detection
- Tangle and clumping detection
- AI-monitoring behavior and sensitivity
- Recovery options
- Warnings about disabled checks
- Explicit Send control

### Why the agent cannot decide this alone

This is where digital assumptions become a real physical operation. The chosen printer may be occupied, prepared with another plate, located remotely, or loaded with valuable material.

Some monitoring options also involve privacy, camera use, false-positive tolerance, or printer-specific limitations.

### What the agent should do

Perform the preflight, recommend safe defaults, and block obviously inconsistent jobs. The user should see a concise checklist and start the send themselves.

---

## 2.10 Live printing and device control

This surface answers: **What is happening now, and can the user intervene?**

OrcaSlicer’s Device surface demonstrates that an AI slicer is also partly a printer-control product.

### What should remain immediately accessible

- Camera
- Job progress
- Current layer and remaining time
- Printer state
- Nozzle and bed temperatures
- Important fan or light controls
- Health and fault alerts
- Pause
- Resume
- Stop

Manual movement, homing, detailed fan control, storage, and file management can be contextual or expert functions.

### Why the agent cannot control this invisibly

Sensors and vision systems can be wrong. Users may notice a sound, smell, obstruction, detaching part, or safety concern that the system cannot observe.

Pause and stop are human override mechanisms. They should never be hidden inside a conversation or require the agent’s cooperation.

### What the agent should do

Monitor the job, explain anomalies, recommend intervention, and automatically pause only under rules the user set in advance. It should clearly report why an automatic intervention occurred.

---

## 2.11 Calibration and troubleshooting

This surface answers: **Is the printer-material combination behaving as expected?**

The audit found both guided calibration pages and more advanced generators.

### Relevant calibration capabilities

- Flow dynamics
- Flow rate
- Temperature
- Pressure advance
- Retraction
- Maximum volumetric speed
- VFA
- Junction deviation
- Input-shaping frequency and damping

### Why the agent cannot completely own calibration

Calibration depends on physical evidence:

- Filament may be wet.
- Adhesion may be poor.
- Transparent or reflective filament may confuse optical sensors.
- A nozzle may be worn or partially obstructed.
- A user may judge two samples differently.
- Automatic measurements contain uncertainty.
- An apparently better surface may reduce strength or accuracy elsewhere.

### What the agent should do

The agent should:

1. Diagnose the observed symptom.
2. Decide whether calibration is justified.
3. Select the appropriate test.
4. Choose safe test ranges.
5. Explain what to observe.
6. Analyze sensor data or photographs.
7. Recommend a result.
8. Say what was saved to the printer or filament profile and that it can be changed back.

The user should not be presented with every calibration parameter unless manual control is requested.

---

## 2.12 Privacy, updates, portability, and expert administration

These functions are used less frequently, but they are important for particular users and organizations.

### User-owned decisions

- Cloud login region
- Stealth or offline mode
- Network-plugin use
- Preset synchronization
- Multi-device management
- Firmware and application update timing
- Camera and monitoring privacy
- Backup and recovery policy
- Importing and replacing configurations
- Ownership and export of project data

### Capabilities that should remain available

- Import 3MF, STL, STEP, SVG, OBJ, AMF, ZIP archives, and configurations
- Export models, projects, sliced plates, G-code, and preset bundles
- Export printer, filament, and process profiles
- Manage downloaded and stored printer files
- Access timelapses
- Run network diagnostics
- Open configuration data
- Enable developer tools

### Why the agent cannot decide these alone

These choices affect privacy, compatibility, organizational policy, intellectual property, and the user’s ability to leave the product.

The agent can simplify the workflows, but it should not silently enable cloud communication, install firmware, replace profiles, or trap projects in a proprietary format.

---

# 3. Recommended final product structure

The application should use one main window rather than turning every stage of a print into equal global navigation.

## 3.1 Home

Home is the hub for:

- Printer cards showing availability, condition, and loaded filament
- Project gallery, open, and project status
- Import of 3MF, STL, STEP, SVG, OBJ, AMF, and ZIP files
- Entry to project versions and backups
- Launching Monitor

## 3.2 Project window

The Project window contains the print-planning lifecycle without dividing it into equal destinations:

- **Prepare:** dominant workspace containing intent, objects and plates, the 3D canvas, geometry editing, local meaning, and the agent plan
- **Check print:** temporary sliced-verification mode
- **Project details:** drawer for authoritative project knowledge
- **Print:** entry point to Send preflight

Prepare may point to Printer Configuration, but it does not own machine calibration, filament inventory, maintenance, or privacy settings.

## 3.3 Printer Configuration

Printer Configuration owns:

- Target printer, nozzle, and build-plate configuration
- Loaded filament, material colors, AMS, and multi-material inventory
- Calibration workflows
- Troubleshooting and maintenance
- Firmware-update timing
- Camera and monitoring privacy
- Network plugins and diagnostic tools
- Stored printer files and timelapses

Prepare displays a compact pointer to this state and surfaces mismatches; it does not duplicate the complete configuration UI.

## 3.4 Monitor

Monitor is a pop-out surface so it can remain visible while the user works elsewhere. It owns:

- Camera
- Progress, current layer, and remaining time
- Printer state
- Nozzle and bed temperatures
- Health and fault alerts
- Pause, Resume, and Stop as never-hidden human overrides

Manual movement, homing, detailed fan or light control, storage, and file management are contextual.

## 3.5 Overlays and application-level layers

- **Send preflight:** final job, destination, material mapping, safety, and monitoring confirmation followed by explicit Send
- **Expert layer:** raw process settings, numeric per-object and per-region overrides, manual calibration ranges, toolpath diagnostics, and G-code
- **Preferences:** cloud region, stealth/offline behavior, network plugins, sync, updates, privacy, backup and recovery, import/export administration, and developer tools

This structure preserves the lifecycle of a print without turning Setup, Intent, Plan, Verify, Print, Monitor, and Diagnose into nine equal screens.

---

# 4. Visibility hierarchy

## 4.1 Default

Continuously visible in the ordinary Project window:

- Project name and saved/unsaved state
- Current printer, nozzle, plate, and material summary
- Compact intent summary
- Compact active plate and object summary
- 3D Prepare canvas
- Add, remove, select, move, rotate, scale, place on face, arrange, duplicate, Undo, and Redo
- Compact agent plan
- Highest unresolved assumption or risk
- Check print and Print

Inside Check, the default changes to sliced appearance, time, material, cost, the highest-priority warning, and comparison with intent. When supports exist, support placement and removal risk become the default Check emphasis.

## 4.2 Contextual

Shown when the project or current task makes it relevant:

- Full object, part, and plate tree
- Per-object material or extruder
- Modifiers, support enforcers, blockers, print order, and search
- Local surface annotations and object-specific requirements
- Mirror, cut, split, merge, assemble, text, measure, repair, positive/negative parts, and multi-plate distribution
- Seam, bridge, overhang, thin-feature, first-layer, island, and collision inspection
- Material changes, purge waste, prime tower, and extruder assignments
- Time and material estimate in Prepare after a valid background slice exists
- Assembly instructions, accessories, and reference pictures
- Calibration and maintenance recommendations
- Firmware updates, storage, timelapses, and multi-device management

## 4.3 On demand

Available through Project details, More, or the expert layer:

- Full intent questionnaire after it has been completed
- Project description, author, license, pictures, BOM, assembly guide, and profile notes
- Version, backup, ownership, and export administration
- Detailed agent rationale, alternatives, confidence, profile deviations, and change history
- Individual speeds and accelerations
- Exact line widths
- Infill and support implementation parameters
- Retraction, wiping, cooling, and purge details
- Complete toolpath legend and playback
- Raw G-code
- Manual calibration ranges
- Network tests, configuration folders, developer mode, and visualization preferences

## 4.4 Interruptive

Normally hidden, but presented prominently at the point where the user can resolve it:

- Wrong printer, nozzle, plate, or filament
- Safety or usage instruction relevant to the current plan
- Unsupported, missing, or defective geometry
- Support entering a protected region
- Violated dimensional requirement
- Material incompatible with the stated use
- Agent uncertainty about a meaning-changing geometry operation
- License conflict during sharing, publishing, commercial use, or export
- Unsaved work, recovery issue, or version conflict
- Printer-health or safety alert

---

# 5. The final design rule

For every OrcaSlicer control, ask four questions:

1. **Does this require physical information the software may not possess?**
   Keep a user confirmation surface.

2. **Does this depend on the object’s purpose, meaning, or the user’s taste?**
   Keep an intent, annotation, or direct-editing surface.

3. **Does this start a consequential, legal, private, or physical action?**
   Keep explicit user control.

4. **Is this merely a technical method for achieving an already-understood goal?**
   Let the agent manage it and expose it only when explanation or expert control is needed.

That rule preserves the genuinely human parts of OrcaSlicer while allowing the agent to remove most of its parameter complexity.

result.output:
## Decide whether this should be a tool

Add or extend a tool when the Agent needs one of three things: up-to-date state read straight from OrcaSlicer, a calculation that OrcaSlicer does and that always gives the same answer for the same input, or a change to the live project.

Do not add a tool for:

- a single setting key. Setting keys are records that the generic settings tools search and edit;
- general printing advice that the model can work out from a skill;
- a fixed bundle of changes such as "make it stronger", where the right answer depends on the part and on what the user cares about;
- driving the UI, such as pressing a button or operating a widget or a hidden panel;
- data that an existing tool already returns in a size-limited result;
- a capability someone might want in the future, with no eval or user task behind it; or
- an operation that the real workspace adapter cannot truly perform through the OrcaSlicer class that owns it.

A fixed, mechanical step of a workflow can be a tool. Examples are generating OrcaSlicer's calibration geometry and starting OrcaSlicer's slice action. Advice should stay a skill until there is a separately specified operation behind it that always behaves the same way.

## Skills versus tools

A skill is text the model reads. A tool is something the app executes. To decide which one a candidate is, ask one question: does it have to run, or does it only have to be read?

- It has to run if it reads state the model does not have, computes something only OrcaSlicer can compute, or changes the project. That makes it a tool.
- It only has to be read if it is judgement, the order to do things in, facts about printing, how to interpret a tool's result, or which question to ask first. That makes it a skill.

The section above covers tools. This section covers skills, and decides the cases that fall in between.

A skill contains things the model could do by itself if it had the right knowledge. It contains nothing that executes. Examples:

- judging evidence, such as telling an adhesion failure from wet filament in a photo;
- the order of a series of tool calls, and the reasons for that order. For "make it stronger": read the settings, change walls and infill, slice, read the report;
- facts about printing, such as what PETG tolerates;
- which question to ask when the answer would change the plan.

A skill is a file on the Agent page, `AgentUI/src/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`: frontmatter with its `name` and a `trigger`, a `description` or both, then the text the model gets. The page sends every skill once per connection with the `skills` bridge message. A skill with a trigger is the app's: when the event it names happens, the host adds it to the one request where the model first reads about the event, as the request's last item, and to no later request. A skill with a description is the model's: `skill_read` lists the described skills in its own description and returns one by name, and is offered only while at least one exists (none does yet). Four skills have triggers, one file each:

- `file-loaded` (trigger `file_loaded`): the first message after a file is opened or imported is a judgement about the load report. It fires when the person opens or drops a file, after an in-app `object_import` (and a failed `project_open`) in the same turn, and in the opened project's chat after an in-app `project_open`, which replaces the conversation and so ends the turn that asked. An MCP client's loads fire nothing. The host sends a picture of the active plate with it and, when no purpose is recorded, one sentence of its own built from that state.
- `project-setup-changed` (trigger `setup_changed`): check the setup in force against the print's purpose. It fires on the result of an in-app `setup_record` that recorded a purpose for the first time or changed its fields (its result says which in `purposeChange`; a call that only restates the title to change the plan does not fire it), when the printer, filament, process or plate type differs from the setup the model was last asked to check under a recorded purpose (on the next tool result of the turn, or on the next turn's first request when the person changed it by hand), and on a turn's first request after the person restored an earlier version while a purpose is recorded. Each time the model is asked to check, the app saves the setup in force as the one checked. The model's own successful `printer_setup` fires nothing: the setup it chose is saved as checked at once (Kenneth, 2026-10-19), so the skill is for a setup that moved without the model, and a pairing its change breaks is caught by the slice-refusal facts and skill. It gives way to the file-loaded skill on a request that carries both, since that skill already asks for the same check.
- `slice-failed` (trigger `slice_failed`): a plate's last slice did not succeed, because OrcaSlicer's check refused the plate or the run failed. The adapter records why on the plate (`WorkspacePlate::slice_failure`: refused or failed, OrcaSlicer's words, the setting and object when named) at the moment it happens (a hook in `Plater::reslice`, `Workspace/SliceRequests.hpp`, and the run's completion event), worded by the print-issue monitor's `slice_failure_of`, and keeps it until the plate slices. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceFailure`; `slice_report` of an unsliced plate adds the check code and the object's name. The skill fires once per failure, on the first request that carries it: the result of the model's own `slice_start`, the turn the app starts when a slice the model started fails after its turn, or the next message after the person's Slice all. The same refusal again is the same failure.
- `print-issues` (trigger `print_issues`): what the print-issue chip's two buttons ask for and how to read what OrcaSlicer reports. The adapter reads a slice's warnings through the monitor's `slice_warnings_of` while the plate is active and keeps a summary on the plate while that slice is current (`WorkspacePlate::slice_warnings`: the count, how many the person ignored, and the first warning, critical first, in OrcaSlicer's words with its setting and object). It counts every warning the chip lists, so the bed-temperature warning too, which `slice_report` leaves out. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceWarnings`. The skill fires on the request that carries a chip's message, and on the first request whose workspace shows warnings no request has carried yet, whether the person sliced (their next message) or the model did (the tool result that shows them, or the app's turn when its slice ended after its turn); a re-slice with the same warnings fires nothing.

The cases in between:

- **A procedure made of existing tool calls.** It is a skill for as long as carrying it out takes judgement. It becomes a tool only when the steps are fixed and the person wants the whole thing as one action that can be undone. If there are many such fixed sequences, they go in one workflow registry (see [When resources or skills are appropriate](#when-resources-or-skills-are-appropriate)).
- **An analysis.** It is a tool when OrcaSlicer computes it and always gets the same answer, such as overhang angles from geometry. It is a skill when it is a judgement about evidence. Pair that skill with the tool that supplies the evidence (`view_render`, `slice_report`).
- **Large reference data.** When the model needs only one part of the data, make it a tool that returns the part an argument selects, as `settings_search` does. When the model needs to see all of the data before it can use any of it, make it text. The printer list described under [Input design](#input-design) is the case we measured: putting the whole list in the instructions worked better than the search tool.
- **A tool description versus a skill.** A tool description says when to call that one tool, in the words a person would use. A skill says how several tools fit together and what to conclude from their results. If a tool description has grown into a step-by-step procedure, move the procedure out into a skill.

When you are not sure, start with a skill. A skill is a text file that ships with the page. A tool costs the whole implementation sequence described below, including fakes, tests, and rebase evidence. Turn a skill into a tool only on the kind of evidence every tool starts from (see [Start with an eval failure](#start-with-an-eval-failure)). Either transcripts show the model getting the sequence wrong in ways that better text does not fix, or the action needs something only the app can give: all-or-nothing application, validation, or undo. The opposite sign exists too. If a skill has turned into exact values and calls in a fixed order, with no judgement between them, it should be written as a tool.

How something gets loaded into the model's context does not decide whether it is a skill or a tool. Today a skill costs its one line in the instructions, and a tool costs its definition on the first request of a conversation (see [Tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)). If we later use the model platform's deferred loading, both will cost one index line plus a load when needed. A skill could then be a deferred read-only tool: the tool's description is the skill's index line, and the tool's result is the skill's text. Tools and skills would then be found the same way and covered by the same eval.

## Prefer extending nouns over multiplying verbs

The settings workflow has four operations that do not change. They work on searchable data, whichever preset layer the values belong to:

```text
settings_search → settings_get → settings_preview_patch → settings_apply_patch
```

Do not create one tool per setting:


#####
| Coordinator | stale session/revision, cancellation race, terminal result |
| Real adapter | live Orca owner, GUI parity, truthful undo/reset/revert behavior, slicing invalidation/completion, document replacement |
| OpenAI adapter | canonical schema projection and successful continuation |
| MCP adapter | canonical schema/output projection, bounded response, protocol errors, disconnect behavior |
| Shell/eval | real project and intended client complete the user task |

If a layer does not apply, say why in the PR. If something cannot be tested, state that openly as a limitation. It is not permission to leave out evidence without saying so.

## Candidate catalog

This catalog lists the tools the finished product would have. It was worked out one product screen at a time from [Designing an AI-Piloted OrcaSlicer](orca-feature-discovery.md), and shaped by the rules under [tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape). Nothing in it is implemented unless the catalog record above says so. Every row still needs what this guide requires of any tool: the eval failure, the trace of its owner, and the test matrix. The number that matters is how many definitions load per turn, not the total. The total here is 36. All of them load on every turn until the measurements under [tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape) justify deferral. The toolsets below are the groups that would be deferred together when that day comes. Until then they only group tools for naming and for delivery.

These conventions apply to every row:

- Every read returns `sessionId` and `revision`.
- Every write that is revision-sensitive takes `expectedRevision`.
- A handle for a detected face or hole carries the revision it was computed at. After the revision moves, using the handle fails with `feature_expired`.
- Facts carry provenance, as defined under [JusPrin-owned project state](#jusprin-owned-project-state).
- Long-running rows follow [Asynchronous operations](#asynchronous-operations). They return an action handle, and the handle's state is read from the `slicing` section of `workspace_inspect`.
- Every read states a fixed maximum size and has a flag that says when the result was cut short.

In the Class column, **R** means read-only, **M** means mutation, and **D** means destructive.

| `core` | 10 | Every turn: state, geometry facts, settings, intent, plan, slicing. |

## Production integration boundaries

### Shell host

The shell is the JusPrin window frame around OrcaSlicer's content. Build one shell, in files this fork owns, and attach it to `MainFrame` in one small place. Decisions about what happens at startup go in a bootstrap or a shell factory that the fork owns. Do not spread environment checks through OrcaSlicer's constructors.

The first production version may still construct OrcaSlicer's old top bar, tab panel, Sidebar, and `GUI_ObjectList` where existing OrcaSlicer behavior depends on them. Leave them out of the visible layout. Do not hide them behind a separate top-level window. Stopping them from being constructed at all is a separate project, because it changes object lifetimes.

### Build registration

List JusPrin's source files explicitly in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/sources.cmake`. OrcaSlicer's central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt` should pull that file in with one include line that never changes. The fork should not keep adding its own files to OrcaSlicer's list.

### Workspace boundary

The workspace API is the typed C++ interface JusPrin uses to read and change the project. The production version should keep the ideas from the proof of concept (POC) that worked:

- separate types for plate IDs and object IDs, so one cannot be passed where the other is expected;
- read-only snapshots of the project;
- explicit errors from commands;
- typed reasons that say what kind of change happened;
- a revision number that only goes up;
- subscriptions that end automatically when the object holding them is destroyed, and that can be moved but not copied.

Before production use, the API must also:

- say which calls must run on the GUI thread;
- say exactly when the revision number goes up;
- explicitly mark the old session's IDs invalid when a project is replaced;
- notice changes that did not go through the adapter (the JusPrin class that implements this API on top of OrcaSlicer);
- report undo and redo availability whether or not any particular widget is visible;
- report whether an undo or redo really changed OrcaSlicer's state;
- not depend on `GUI_ObjectList` for commands that change the model;
- offer plate selection, object import and addition, and the other commands the product needs;
- keep wxWidgets types and OrcaSlicer types out of its public interface.

Sometimes the operation you need exists only inside OrcaSlicer's UI code. In that case, add the smallest possible command to the OrcaSlicer class that already does the work, and name it for what it does. Do not copy the operation into JusPrin. Do not fake clicks or key presses on hidden controls.

### Canvas presentation

`GLCanvas3D` keeps a small API for controlling how its parts are presented. That API contains nothing specific to JusPrin. A controller in fork-owned code uses the API to apply JusPrin's choices, and puts OrcaSlicer's previous state back when the controller is destroyed. Whether a control is drawn and whether it receives input must be two separate switches. Otherwise a control that is hidden could still swallow pointer events. OrcaSlicer's native gizmos (the on-canvas tools such as Move and Rotate) must stay usable while one is active.

The POC had one broad switch, `render_overlays`. Production needs finer control. Treat each of these as its own item that can be shown or hidden separately: OrcaSlicer's main toolbar, the gizmo picker, the handles of the active gizmo, plate actions, object labels, layer-editing controls, navigation aids, the Preview legend, and the Preview sliders. Some controls are shared between canvases, such as `Plater`'s collapse toolbar. A shared control must be saved and restored by one object that lives as long as the shell does. Do not give each canvas its own guard for it.

### Plates and Project pane

This pane is native code owned by the fork (`Shell/LeftPane`). It sits to the left of the workspace on Prepare. Its first tab lists every plate, even when the project has only one. Its second tab shows the saved project's identity, the model's 3MF metadata, the history of physical prints, the version history, and export. The pane keeps no project state of its own and has no undo of its own. It draws what two model classes describe, and those classes do not depend on the GUI. Every click calls a workspace command.

| Piece | What it is responsible for |
|---|---|
| `Workspace/ProjectOutline.hpp`, `IWorkspace::outline()` | The data the pane reads: plates, copies of objects (each with the plate that holds it), volumes, facts about customization and the mesh, and what is selected below the object level. Which plate a copy is on comes from `PartPlateList`. The code never guesses it from where the copy sits. |
| `Shell/LeftPaneModel` | Which rows the Plates tab shows, and when. The active plate is open. Other plates are folded, each with a summary computed from its current copies. A row has child rows only when there is data for them. "Not on a plate" appears only when some copy is on no plate. This class also handles switching between the tabs and between the views inside the Project tab. |
| `Shell/ProjectPaneModel` | The contents of the Details and Print history views, as plain data. A field that nobody filled in is left out. The slicer's time estimate and the measured print duration are kept as separate values. A ledger record that has nothing to display is included in the count but gets no row. |
| `Workspace/OrcaOutline.cpp` | The commands, implemented on top of OrcaSlicer: `select_plate`, `add_plate`, `select_copy`, `select_volume`, `plate_actions`, `run_plate_action`. Each command ends by calling the same code OrcaSlicer's own UI calls (`Plater::select_plate_by_hover_id`, the toolbar's Add plate event, `Selection` plus the canvas's object-select event). The events are raised synchronously on the GUI thread, so the change has already happened when the command returns. |
| `Shell/LeftPane`, `LeftPaneProject.cpp` | Drawing and input. While drawing, the pane records where each control ended up. Pointer handling looks each click up in that record, so a click can only hit something that was actually drawn. |

The ledger is the record of physical prints. It can have any number of subscribers, through `ProjectPersistence::subscribe_ledger`. The pane and the header's overflow menu each subscribe to it separately.

### Print issues and OrcaSlicer's notifications

Inside the shell OrcaSlicer's own notifications are held but not drawn. JusPrin reads the list back and draws what it holds: print problems as a status pill in the canvas's lower right corner, the list it opens, and a bubble beside the object the selected issue is about, with **Ask AI** and **Resolve with AI**; the outcome of an action (export finished, an arrange that was refused) as a short confirmation above the pill; and work that is still running (a slice, an arrange, an export) as an entry in the chat.

**OrcaSlicer's notification list is the source of truth.** A notification carries a kind, a level and words. It does not carry the object it is about, so where OrcaSlicer lets its check be asked again, that check is asked once more for the object only.

| Piece | Owns |
|---|---|
| `PrintIssues/NoticeKinds` | Where each of OrcaSlicer's notification kinds goes: the issue list, a confirmation, running work, application state, or nowhere. Every kind is named; a kind OrcaSlicer adds stops the build in this file until someone routes it. |
| `PrintIssues/PrintIssueMonitor` | Reads the list on the notification manager's own turn, compares it with what it saw last, and rebuilds only on a change. Asks OrcaSlicer's checks for the object behind a validation, a copy over the plate's edge, an object out of a nozzle's reach and a slicing step warning. Holds no rule about what a problem is. |

---
name: print-issues
trigger: print_issues
---

# Issues I report about the print

The rules above still apply. This request is the first to carry something I reported about the print: the person pressed a button on a print-issue chip (their message has a <print_issue> block), or a slice finished with warnings that plate's last slice did not have (the plate's sliceWarnings, in the workspace and in a tool result's slicing section; slice_report's findings section has the full list, except the heatbed warning and a repeated timelapse one).

The chip's buttons: "Explain this issue and my options." is a question, so answer it and leave the project as it is. "Help fix this issue." asks you to change what the issue names, and only that; anything else worth changing is a suggestion.

How to read a finding. A blocker means I will not slice or print until it is fixed; a warning means the slice exists and can print; a critical warning is one I flag as serious. The setting key names what to change, and settings_search or settings_get with that key tells what the setting is and its value now. The object, when named, narrows where; with none it is about the plate or the setup. count says how many warnings there are; read slice_report's findings when more than the first matters. An ignored one is a finding the person chose not to be told about again: still true of the slice. Explain a finding from its words, never from a cause you supply.

A warning is my statement about the slice, not proof the print will fail. Say what it risks for this print and its purpose. Some are the person's call because they trade the look, the time or their hardware: adding support (marks on the surface, clean-up), re-orienting, a filament pairing, a nozzle. A setting that only shapes the toolpath is yours to settle when the request covers it.

A finding counts as resolved only when a new slice no longer reports it, never because a setting changed or a chip was closed or ignored. Asked whether the print is ready, name what the slice still warns about.

| What I report while slicing | What it usually means, and where it points |
| --- | --- |
| "It seems object … has floating regions / floating cantilever / large overhangs. Please re-orient the object or enable support generation."; "Your model needs support!" | Parts start in the air or overhang far and will sag or fail without support. Support settings (enable_support, support_type) or orientation; which one is the person's call. |
| "Object can't be printed for empty layer between … and …" (critical) | Layers with nothing printed: features thinner than a line, or a broken mesh. object_analyze, object_repair, layer height or line widths. |
| "… is too close to others, and collisions may be caused."; "Prime Tower is too close to others"; "too close to exclusion area" | The nozzle or head may hit an object, the tower or a no-go area. Position (object_place, plate_layout) or print_sequence. |
| "Found gcode path conflicts between object … and …" (critical) | Two objects' paths cross. Spacing or layout. |
| "A G-code path goes beyond the plate boundaries." / "… beyond the max print height." | A skirt, brim, support or the object itself leaves the printable area by a little (more is a blocker). Position, brim_width, skirt_distance or size. |
| Speed, acceleration, jerk or junction deviation above the printer's maximum ("Orca will automatically cap …"); "Setting the jerk speed too low …" | It prints with the motion capped to the printer's limits. The setting named, or the printer's machine_max_* values. |
| A support base pattern replaced ("Rectilinear will be used instead") | I substitute a pattern this support type cannot use. support_base_pattern. |
| "Partial flushing volume set to 0 …"; "PLA and PETG filaments detected in the mixture …"; filament shrinkage or XY size compensation "will not be used"; different nozzle and filament diameters with the prime tower | Multi-filament settings: colours may mix, or a setting is dropped for this plate. Flushing volumes, the filaments chosen, the setting named. |
| "The current heatbed temperature is relatively high. The nozzle may clog when printing this filament in a closed environment. …" | The bed is at or above the filament's softening point; in a shut enclosure the heat can soften it before the nozzle. Opening the door or removing the top glass is the person's call; or lower this plate type's bed temperature. |
| "The nozzle hardness required by the filament is higher than …" | An abrasive filament wears the installed nozzle. Physical, the person's call: nozzle or filament. |
| Traditional timelapse "may cause surface imperfections"; smooth timelapse with the prime tower off | Only for a print that records a timelapse. timelapse_type, enable_prime_tower. |

I raise no slicing warning for thin walls, bridges, bed adhesion, brims or cooling. When the person asks about those, read slice_report's firstLayer, islands and supports sections and the settings; never present one as a warning I gave.

([[figma-jusprin-v2-file]]). Since 2026-10-20 these artifacts ARE the source of truth ([[design-source-is-claude-artifacts]]); edit them directly. The Figma re-sync steps below are history.

1. Design System: https://claude.ai/artifact/3zgiix8rAw3rXextQnR5UL (version 9)
   - `tokens.json` + `tokens.css`, 37 coded React components (`window.JusPrin`).
   - Each component card: every variant Figma draws, a Light and a Dark panel,
     then the coded component. The page lists them as one flat table in bundle
     order with code names; it draws no group headings.
   - `screens/<page>/<screen>.spec.txt` (166) + `screens/index.json`: plain
     files for agents, one resolved line per layer.
2. Design canvas "JusPrin v2": https://claude.ai/artifact/VCEppdwfT7v32W4beUxL1v
   (version 7): 10 pages with Figma's names in Figma's order, 198 artboards at
   their Figma x,y and in Figma's layer order, each drawn in the Light or Dark
   mode Figma sets on it; "… · Light & Dark" review frames are drawn whole.

Tools, reads and backups are durable now, outside the repo:
`~/.claude/projects/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/figma-mirror/` — start with
its `README.md` (step-by-step re-sync). `published/` is an exact copy of what is
live; `backup-2026-10-13-before-reimport/` holds the earlier state with the
scripts that reproduce it byte for byte.

How Kenneth wants a re-sync done (2026-10-13): back up first, re-import, then
compare the backup with the new import so nothing already in sync regresses.
The method that worked, in order:
- rebuild from the old reads and require byte-identical output (proves the
  scripts);
- re-read Figma with the old script and diff the reads (proves Figma unchanged:
  all 14 files were identical);
- only then change scripts, and explain every file `compare_builds.py` reports;
- score every artboard against Figma's own page screenshots
  (`visual_compare.py`) and allow no artboard to score worse.
Result of that run: 0 artboards further from Figma, 36 closer; boards within 5
of Figma (0–255 scale) went from 99 to 122 of 186; all 37 cards and 163 of 166
spec files came out byte-identical; tokens matched Figma's variables exactly.

What the screenshot comparison caught that file checks could not: dark panels I
had added behind dark variants (Figma has none), frames forced dark by a "dark"
in their name (use Figma's `explicitVariableModes` instead), a frame half light
and half dark through a nested mode, sets whose background is a two-stop linear
gradient, Figma's GRID layout (children need their own positions), and small
frames centred in the 40px-minimum artboard instead of top-left.

Other traps: an absolutely positioned layer followed by in-flow siblings paints
over them in HTML (give the later siblings `position:relative`); Figma tints
icons with a mask plus a coloured rectangle; the Artifact tool's bulk read
prints small text files into context, so have a background agent do large
backups; a session scratchpad is wiped on restart — never keep the only copy of
tools there; when two reads of a page exist, keep the later one by timestamp.

scores are all such screens); radial and image fills are placeholders; Figma

input.description: Check on-demand skills, whether Orca's calibration dialogs save results, and the printer panel's manual door into Orca settings

content.text:
I read the fork's product docs, then traced OrcaSlicer's two calibration implementations and every JusPrin surface where a calibration entry could live. Nothing was changed. Here is the brainstorm.

## What the docs commit to

Calibration is surface 9 of the nine the product keeps, "Calibration and troubleshooting". The product definition puts it under **Printer Configuration**, not Prepare: Prepare "does not own machine calibration" and only shows a pointer and mismatches. Visibility is "contextual" for recommendations and "on demand" for manual ranges. The agent's job is listed as eight steps: diagnose the symptom, decide whether calibration is justified, pick the test, choose safe ranges, explain what to look at, analyze a photo or sensor data, recommend a value, and say what was saved and that it can be undone. The person never sees every parameter unless they ask for manual control.

The tool guide already reserves two tools, `calibration_list` (read) and `calibration_generate` (mutating, "onto a new plate"), at priority 2, and says applying a result reuses the existing filament-scope settings tools with a saved copy. Its third eval is exactly this flow: stringing, temperature tower, photo, apply. The architecture's implementation order puts calibration in step 7, after Monitor and preflight.

## What OrcaSlicer actually has

Two separate implementations, and they behave very differently:

- **The SoftFever dialogs** in [calib_dlg.cpp](src/slic3r/GUI/calib_dlg.cpp) cover temperature, flow, pressure advance, retraction, max volumetric speed, VFA, input shaping and cornering. Each one ends in a `Plater::calib_*` call, and every one of those starts with `new_project()`. The test replaces whatever project is open, edits the live print and filament presets, and sets a calibration mode on the slicing process. The person slices and prints as normal, reads the print by eye, and types the winning value into the filament profile themselves. Nothing is saved automatically.
- **The Bambu wizard** behind the hidden Calibration tab ([CalibrationWizard.cpp](src/slic3r/GUI/CalibrationWizard.cpp), [CalibUtils.cpp](src/slic3r/Utils/CalibUtils.cpp)) never touches the open project. It builds the test model off-screen, sends it straight to a connected Bambu machine, reads measured pressure-advance and flow results back from the firmware, and its Save page writes them. It covers only pressure advance and flow, and only on a connected Bambu printer.

The shared pieces are in `libslic3r/calib.hpp`: the test modes, the parameter struct, and the pattern generator. I did not run `git blame`, so I'm treating all of this as upstream OrcaSlicer on the basis of the file names and the "SoftFever calibrations" comments.

Nothing in fork-owned code mentions calibration today. Whether Orca's own Calibration menu is still reachable inside the shell is unverified.

## Where it could go

**Entry points.** The fork already has the right doors, and they all lead to a conversation rather than a wizard, which matches the decision that replaced the Add-printer dialog with a chat:

1. The printer: the Home card's kebab and the in-project printer chip menu both have "Printer settings…", which opens the temporary printer conversation in `PrinterPanel` with a mode enum of Add, Change, Connect. A fourth mode, Calibrate, is the smallest change and sits exactly where the product definition says calibration lives.
2. The filament: most tests (temperature, flow, pressure advance, retraction, volumetric speed) are really about one printer-and-filament pair, and their results land in filament settings. The filament chip already opens a filament chat through the same panel. "Calibrate this filament…" there may be the entry people actually reach for. Input shaping and cornering belong to the printer.
3. A symptom: the person types "stringing" in the project chat or presses Ask AI on a print issue. That is the diagnosis step. The project chat should decide calibration is justified and hand off, not run it, because of the constraint below.

**The constraint that shapes everything: the test print replaces the project.** Orca's generators call `new_project()`. That conflicts with the tool guide's "onto a new plate", and I'd expect it to conflict badly: the generators change print and filament presets for the whole project and set a slicing-wide calibration mode, so a calibration plate next to real plates would contaminate them. That is a hypothesis from reading the code, not something I tested. Three ways out:

- Accept it. A calibration becomes its own managed project ("Nozzle temperature test, PLA on X1C"), visible in the Home gallery, with its own chat. This is what Orca's code does, so it needs no reimplementation. The person's real project is autosaved and one click away.
- Use the Bambu off-screen path through a tool when the printer is a connected Bambu. The project is untouched and results are measured, not eyeballed. Narrow coverage.
- Write a fork-owned generator that drops geometry into a plate. This breaks the "do not reimplement" rule and would re-create the preset contamination problem anyway. I'd rule it out.

My recommendation is the first, with the second layered on for Bambu.

**Where the logic goes**, following the page-first rule and the skills-versus-tools test:

- Tools, because they must run: `calibration_list` reads which tests fit this printer and filament, safe ranges, whether the machine can self-measure, and stored machine results. `calibration_generate` wraps `Plater::calib_*` or the Bambu path and returns the project it made. Saving a result needs no new tool: filament-scope `settings_apply_patch` with a saved copy already exists and the printer panel already uses that pattern.
- A skill, because it is judgement: a description-based calibration skill read through `skill_read`, in the same shape as [print-issues/SKILL.md](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/skills/print-issues/SKILL.md). It holds the symptom-to-test table, ranges by material, what to photograph, how to read a tower, and which setting the result goes in. The print-issues skill gains one line pointing at it for material symptoms.
- The page: cards in AgentUI for the chosen test and ranges, "print it, then send me a photo", and a result receipt with Save and Undo, mirroring the added-printer receipt.
- The shell: no new window. The design canvas has no calibration boards yet; they would belong on its "Printer & Material Settings" page, which is a later design task.

## Decisions that are yours

- Whether leaving the project for a calibration project is acceptable, or whether a non-destructive path is required. That changes the architecture, not just the UI.
- The first batch of tests. I'd start with temperature, flow and pressure advance, the three people ask about and that end in filament settings.
- Where results are saved: a named filament copy, as the printer panel does, versus the project's filament.
- Whether a calibration print goes into the physical-print ledger. It is a physical print.
- Whether a small product-neutral seam is needed in the Bambu path to generate without sending. `CalibUtils` is static and reaches for the app singleton, so I'd expect so, but that's unverified.

content.text:
Confirmed, by reading the code rather than running it: the generators write to project-wide presets, and OrcaSlicer has no per-plate presets, so a calibration generated into a plate of an existing project would change how every other plate in that project slices. The details also turned up a second constraint that matters for the "calibration as its own project" plan: the calibration behaviour is runtime-only state that is not saved in the 3MF.

**What each generator writes outside its own objects.** Every `Plater::calib_*` function edits `preset_bundle->prints/filaments/printers.get_edited_preset().config`. That is the one edited preset of each kind for the whole open project. Plates have no presets of their own.

| Test | Print preset | Filament preset | Printer preset |
|---|---|---|---|
| Temperature tower ([Plater.cpp:13247](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:13247)) | `enable_wrapping_detection`, `initial_layer_print_height` | `nozzle_temperature`, `nozzle_temperature_initial_layer` | `resonance_avoidance` |
| Flow rate ([Plater.cpp:13033](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:13033)) | `layer_height`, `initial_layer_print_height`, `alternate_extra_wall`, `reduce_crossing_wall`, `enable_wrapping_detection`, `max_volumetric_extrusion_rate_slope` | none | `resonance_avoidance` |
| Pressure advance pattern ([Plater.cpp:12702](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:12702)) | accelerations, jerks, junction deviation, `print_sequence`, `outer_wall_speed`, `line_width`, `initial_layer_line_width`, `initial_layer_speed`, `skirt_loops`, `wall_loops`, `brim_type`, `enable_wrapping_detection` | `filament_retract_when_changing_layer`, `filament_wipe` | `wipe`, `retract_when_changing_layer`, `resonance_avoidance` |

The flow and temperature tests also set per-object settings, and those are confined to the test objects. Only the preset edits above leak. The generators then call `update_dirty` and `reload_config` on the settings tabs, so the project's presets show as modified from that point on.

**The calibration mode itself is per plate, but only in memory.** Each plate owns its own `Print` object, and the generator stores the test's mode and range on the current plate's print. The G-code writer reads it there, for example to step the temperature per layer at [GCode.cpp:4697](src/libslic3r/GCode.cpp:4697). Nothing writes it to the 3MF, and loading a project resets it to none at [Plater.cpp:5891](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:5891). So a saved temperature tower project, reopened later, slices as a plain tower at one temperature. The pressure-advance pattern is the exception: its per-layer commands go into the plate's custom G-code, which the 3MF does save. That pattern also hard-codes the first plate's origin at [Plater.cpp:12814](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:12814), another sign it was never written to run on any plate but the first of a fresh project.

**What this means for the plan you approved.**

- "New plate in the current project", as the tool guide's `calibration_generate` row says, is not viable without rewriting the generators. The guide's row needs correcting when the tool is specified.
- "Own project" works, with one addition: the calibration project is only valid in the session that generated it. The agent's flow has to go from generate to slice to print without the person closing and reopening it. If they do reopen it, the app must regenerate rather than reslice, or treat the saved project as a record only.
- The message you asked for, telling the person what will happen, has to cover both halves: the current project will be closed and autosaved, and the test's presets are temporary and will not be saved into their filament or printer settings. The latter is what Orca's `new_project` confirmation dialog about modified presets asks on the way back, and the fork already auto-answers Orca dialogs on file open, so the return path needs a deliberate answer: discard the calibration's preset edits.
- The sole thing worth saving back is the measured result, through the filament-scope settings tools with a named copy, as you confirmed.

# Figma mirror: tools and backups

> **2026-10-20: Figma is retired and out of date.** The two Claude artifacts are now the up-to-date JusPrin
> design. Do NOT re-sync them from Figma: that would overwrite newer design work. Edit them directly:
> copy the live files into `work/` (or read them with the Artifact tool), change them, publish only the changed
> files, then rsync `work/` into `published/`. Remember the canvas keeps its own copy of the design system in
> `project/ds/jusprin/` (tokens and component styles): change both artifacts together. `tools/composer/` holds
> the scripts used since then (`render.py` screenshots boards with headless Chrome; `resize_board.py` fixes a
> board's height in its file and in `canvas.json`; `build_filament_step.py` draws the Add-a-printer step-3 boards and their spec files, `measure_sheets.py` measures their sheet heights with headless Chrome). Before publishing to either artifact, do a plain `read` of its url: a publish after only `path` reads is refused as "haven't viewed the latest version". The Figma re-sync steps below are kept as history.


This folder keeps what is needed to re-sync two Claude artifacts with the Figma file "JusPrin v2"
(file key `jo9J1sK9ZZ0vxncWnSp0vH`), and to prove a re-sync breaks nothing.

- Canvas "JusPrin v2": https://claude.ai/artifact/VCEppdwfT7v32W4beUxL1v
- JusPrin Design System: https://claude.ai/artifact/3zgiix8rAw3rXextQnR5UL

It lives outside the JusPrin repo on purpose: it is not product code, and untracked files in the repo mean
"unfinished work" there.

## What is here

- `published/` — an exact copy of what is published now (`canvas/project`, `ds/project`). Every re-sync is
  compared against it, then it is replaced by the new build.
- `figma/spec3/<page id>.txt` — the Figma pages as last read (one text line per layer). `figma/vars.json` —
  Figma's variables, text styles and shadows as last read.
- `tools/` — the scripts (below).
- `visual/figma/*.png` — Figma's own screenshot of each page, used to score the artboards.
  `visual/scores-*.json` — the scores before and after the 2026-10-13 re-import.
- `backup-2026-10-13-before-reimport/` — the published files, the Figma reads and the scripts as they were
  before the re-import of 2026-10-13. Running those scripts on those reads reproduces those files byte for byte.

## Re-sync, step by step

1. Read Figma. For each page id (`0:1 1423:396 320:1053 160:59 9:153 359:116 1148:1287 1258:396 1328:2780`)
   call the Figma tool `use_figma` with the text of `tools/spec3_min.js`, replacing `__PAGE__` and `__OFFSET__`
   (0, then 20200, 40400, ... while the offset is below the returned `total`). About 35 calls; have background
   agents make them, because each reply is large. Run `tools/vars.js` once the same way and save its result as
   `figma/vars.json`. The script source is `tools/figma_spec3.js`; `python3 tools/minify.py tools/figma_spec3.js
   tools/spec3_min.js` rebuilds the one-line version.
2. Decode the replies from the session transcripts:
   `SESSION=<session id> OUT=figma python3 tools/collect.py`
3. Build into a scratch folder `new/`:

       export FIGMA_DIR=$PWD/figma DS_DIR=$PWD/new/ds REPO=/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin
       rm -rf new && mkdir new && cp -R published/ds new/ds
       python3 tools/build_variants.py $REPO new/ds
       python3 tools/build_canvas.py $REPO new/canvas <design system version id>
       mkdir -p new/specs/project/screens && cp published/ds/project/tokens.json new/specs/project/
       python3 tools/specs.py $REPO figma/spec3 new/specs/project/screens

4. Compare with what is published: `python3 tools/compare_builds.py published new`. With no change in Figma and
   no change in the scripts, every line must say "identical". Explain every file that is not before publishing.
5. Compare with Figma itself: take a screenshot of each Figma page (`get_screenshot`, maxDimension 8000) into
   `visual/figma/`, then `tools/visual_pages.py`, screenshot each `composite-<page>.html` at full page size,
   and `tools/visual_compare.py`. No artboard may score worse than in `visual/scores-after.json`.
6. Publish only the changed files to the same artifact URLs, check the live pages, then replace `published/`.

## Known limits

Photographs and 3D renders are flat placeholders. Artwork over 64px is not drawn. The page Figma marks obsolete
is not read. Radial and image fills are placeholders (linear gradients are drawn). Figma stacks some dark screens
on top of light ones on "Printer & Material Settings"; the canvas keeps Figma's stacking.
